segments.text: Nel capitolo sei, in una mattina di giugno del milletrecento, Lapo vide passare a cavallo, nella strada della bottega, gli uomini che andavano al confino a Sarzana.
Uno di loro cavalcava un poco davanti agli altri e non guardava niuno: era Guido Cavalcanti, il poeta.
In agosto Guido tornò a Firenze con la febbre delle paludi, e alla fine del mese morì.
Lapo vide passare quelli che lo portavano a seppellire, e cercò fra loro l'amico di Cavalcanti; ma non l'aveva mai visto in faccia.
Quell'amico era Dante Alighieri.
In quei mesi Dante era uno dei priori, e il suo nome era sotto il bando che mandò Guido al confino, con i nomi degli altri priori, sotto lo stesso sigillo.
Nel milletrecentodue il podestà condannò Dante, e Dante non tornò mai più a Firenze.
In esilio scrisse un lungo poema, la Commedia: il viaggio di un uomo vivo per i luoghi dei morti, l'Inferno, il Purgatorio e il Paradiso.
L'uomo vivo è Dante stesso, e con lui va un poeta latino, Virgilio, che Dante chiama maestro e duca.
Dante dice anche quando comincia il viaggio: nei giorni prima di Pasqua, nella primavera del milletrecento.
In quella primavera Lapo era nella bottega dei Cerchi da pochi mesi, e Calendimaggio non era ancora venuto.
Guido Cavalcanti era vivo, e a Firenze.
Così nel poema Guido è vivo; ma quando Dante scriveva, e quando la gente cominciò a leggere i suoi versi, Guido era morto da anni.
Dante lo sapeva, e lo sapeva chi leggeva.
Il canto decimo dell'Inferno parla di parti e di esilio; ma quando il padre di Guido domanda del figlio, tutto sta nel tempo di un verbo.
Nell'Inferno di Dante gli eretici stanno in tombe aperte, piene di fuoco.
In una parte ci sono quelli che seguivano Epicuro e dicevano che l'anima muore con il corpo.
Da una di queste tombe due fiorentini parlano a Dante: Farinata degli Uberti, un ghibellino, e Cavalcante de' Cavalcanti, un guelfo, il padre di Guido.
Leggerai tutto il canto, verso per verso, nel libro di Carl Witte (Berlino, milleottocentosessantadue).
Nel libro di Witte le parole di chi parla non sono fra « »: chi parla, lo dice il verso stesso (Ed io…, disse…).
Dante e Virgilio vanno lungo il muro, fra le tombe aperte degli eretici.
Dante domanda se può vedere quelli che stanno dentro: forse pensa ai fiorentini.

Ora sen va per un secreto calle
Tra il muro della terra e li martìri
Lo mio Maestro, ed io dopo le spalle.

segments.text: Una voce esce da una tomba: è Farinata degli Uberti, il capo dei ghibellini di Firenze quando Dante non era ancora nato.

Dopo Montaperti i capi ghibellini volevano che Firenze non ci fosse più; Farinata solo disse di no, e Firenze restò in piedi.
Morì nel milleduecentosessantaquattro.
Diciannove anni dopo un frate condannò Farinata, già morto, come eretico; gli Uberti, cacciati da Firenze, non tornarono mai più.

O Tosco, che per la città del foco

Nella primavera del milletrecento Guido è vivo: ma che cosa sa di lui suo padre, fra i morti?

grammar.title: Come scrive Dante
grammar.rule: Dante scrive ei, fur, fia, veggiam; oggi si scrive egli, furono, sarà, vediamo.
grammar.note_en:
This lesson asks you to read, not to produce. Dante's Italian is the Florentine of Lapo's shop, bent by metre and rhyme. Most of what looks strange is a short form, an older ending or a word order you know from Latin verse. Read each tercet for its sense first, with the margin; then come back here for the forms.

**Who is speaking.** Witte prints no quotation marks. Dante marks the speaker in the verse: Ed io: …, Ed egli a me: …, Poi disse: …, or puts disse inside the speech, as Latin puts inquit (S'egli han quell'arte, disse, male appresa: 'if they have learned that art badly,' he said). Ed egli a me and Ed io a lui leave out the verb of saying altogether: 'and he [said] to me'.

**Short forms.** Dante's verse is full of shortened words, and the list below gives their modern equivalents, not one rule for making them. Some simply lose a final vowel after l, n or r, as modern prose still does in aver fatto or il signor Rossi: cor = cuore, supin = supino, man = mani, parlar = parlare, veder = vedere, ubbidir = ubbidire, sentier = sentiero, orazion = orazione, cagion = cagione, sol = solo, nobil = nobile, maggior = maggiori. Others are shortened from older endings: fur from furo (= furono), tornar from tornaro (= tornarono), appreser = appresero, pinser = spinsero (from pingere, an older form of spingere). Sien = siano and dicer = dire are older forms, not cuts. The apostrophe marks a vowel dropped before another vowel (com'a, ov'è, viv'egli, Rispos'io), and a few truncated words stand alone with an apostrophe: I' = io, fu' = fui, Prega' = pregai, a' = ai, co' = coi, E' = egli.

**Pronouns.**
- He: egli, ei (Ed ei mi disse), and e' (E' par che voi veggiate: 'it seems that you see', where e' is the empty subject 'it', like French il). Elli, the form many modern editions print, does not occur in Witte's text of this canto.
- Lui without a as an indirect object: Rispos'io lui = risposi a lui ('I answered him'), where Latin has a dative (respondi ei). In Prega' io lui ('I begged him') lui is simply the direct object, as in modern pregai lui and Latin precatus sum eum.
- Li means 'to him' (= gli): Ed io li satisfeci ('and I answered him'). Gli means 'them' (= li): gli dispersi ('I scattered them'). The two had not yet settled into today's roles.
- Il as object 'it, him' before a consonant: tutto il vedrai ('you will see him whole'), che il fei ('that I did it'). Nol = non lo; gliel = glielo or glieli (Non gliel celai: 'I did not hide them from him').
- Meco, teco = con me, con te (Latin mecum, tecum).
- Cui: in a cui posta it means 'whose' ('at whose request'; modern alla cui richiesta). In Forse cui Guido vostro ebbe a disdegno it means 'whom', the object of Guido's disdain; how this cui joins the line before ('he leads me, perhaps, [to] one whom…') is the canto's famous problem (see below).

**Pronouns after the verb.** As in Compagni (lesson 15), an unstressed pronoun follows a verb that opens its clause: Potrebbesi veder? ('could they be seen?'), Piacciati di restare ('may it please you to stay'), Guardommi ('he looked at me'), Dissemi ('he told me'). Clause-initial position is the typical case, not the only one (Potrebbesi follows La gente…). In ordinary modern usage the pronoun follows the verb mainly with imperatives, infinitives and gerunds: the placement in Parlami, satisfammi, Volgiti, solvetemi is still normal, though satisfare and solvere themselves are now literary (modern soddisfami, scioglietemi).

**Verb forms.** The canto's hard verbs are older shapes of verbs you know.
- Remote past: uscio = uscì ('came out': third-person -ì, with an -o added at the end of a line; say uscìo, not the noun uscio 'door'), apersi = aprii ('I opened'), surse = sorse ('rose'), fei = feci ('I did'), furo, fur = furono ('they were'), tornar = tornarono ('they returned'), gimmo = andammo ('we went', from gire), ascose = nascose ('hid'). Prega' and fu' are pregai, fui.
- Present: tegno, vegno = tengo, vengo ('I keep, I come'); face, faci = fa, fai ('does, you do'); fiere, fiede = ferisce ('strikes'; fiede at the end of the canto: 'leads down into'); veggiam = vediamo ('we see'); sapem = sappiamo ('we know'); regge in line 80 is 'rules', but in line 82 it is a different verb: 'may you return' (see below).
- Imperfect: avea, parea, facea = aveva, pareva, faceva; and Ch'io faceva = facevo: the old first person ended in -a, like the third.
- Future: fia = sarà ('will be'), three times: fia raccesa, Fia nostra conoscenza, fia chiusa.
- Subjunctive: sien = siano (Le parole tue sien conte: 'let your words be measured'); veggiate = vediate; La mente tua conservi ('let your mind keep'): a subjunctive used as a command, Latin's jussive.
- Conditional: Potrebbesi, sarei mosso: the -ei type you know. Dante also has an older conditional in -ia (saria = sarebbe, met in chapter 5), common in other cantos; this one happens not to use it.

**Se of wishing.** Twice a speaker opens with se and a subjunctive that is not a condition but a wish offered in exchange: E se tu mai nel dolce mondo regge, / Dimmi… ('so may you one day return to the sweet world: tell me…'); Deh, se riposi mai vostra semenza ('ah, so may your descendants one day have rest'). Compare Latin sic with the subjunctive (sic te diva potens Cypri…). Regge here is Latin redeas: 'may you return'.

**One verb decides the scene.** Dante says of Guido ebbe a disdegno ('held in disdain'), a past tense about Guido's past disdain. The remote past does not itself mean that its subject is dead (Lapo's living friends use it every day); but a Latinist knows how a perfect can close a life (vixerunt; fuimus Troes), and Cavalcante, anxious, hears ebbe so, as speaking of a life already ended: Come / Dicesti: egli ebbe? non viv'egli ancora? Non fiere gli occhi suoi lo dolce lome? ('What? Did you say "he had"? Is he not still alive? Does the sweet light not strike his eyes?'). His own questions are in the present: viv', fiere. Dante pauses: he cannot reconcile the foresight of the dead (Ciacco foretold Florence's troubles in canto VI, lesson 17) with Cavalcante's ignorance of his son's present state; Cavalcante takes the pause for an answer. Only after Farinata's prophecy does Dante ask, and learn, how this can be: the damned see the distant future, but of what is near or present they know only what someone brings them (e s'altri nol ci apporta, 104), and Dante uses that path at once: il suo nato è co' vivi ancor congiunto ('his son is still joined with the living'). Easter 1300 is the date of the journey: Guido is alive inside the poem. When the canto was read he had been dead for years, and the prior who had signed his confinement was the poet.

Who is the cui of line 63 is the most debated question in the canto. The usual readings: Virgil leads Dante perhaps to one whom Guido disdained (Beatrice, or the God she stands for); or Guido disdained Virgil himself, or the Latin poets. The margin gives the first, one common interpretation; what matters for the scene is ebbe.

**Fact and fiction.** Farinata degli Uberti led the Florentine Ghibellines, won at Montaperti by the Arbia (4 September 1260), and, as the chroniclers tell it, alone opposed the destruction of Florence at the council of Empoli that followed; he died in 1264, and in 1283 the inquisitor condemned him and his wife as heretics after their death. The Guelfs were driven out in 1248 and 1260 and came back both times (1251, 1267); the Uberti were excluded from every later return. Cavalcante de' Cavalcanti was a Guelf noble, said by Boccaccio to follow Epicurus; his son Guido had married Farinata's daughter in the peace of the 1260s. The fifty moons of line 79 run from spring 1300 to about the middle of 1304, when the exiles' hopes of return failed (the cardinal's peace mission in the spring, the defeat at the Lastra in July): that is the usual reading. The lady who rules here is Proserpina, queen of the underworld, who was also the moon. Line 132 promises that Beatrice will reveal Dante's life to him; in Paradiso XVII it is his ancestor Cacciaguida who does so, at her prompting. The Cardinal of line 120 is Ottaviano degli Ubaldini, the Ghibelline cardinal; lo secondo Federico is the emperor Frederick II (died 1250). Lapo appears only in the introduction, recalling what chapter 6 showed; nothing in the canto is changed.

The tables set Witte's forms beside today's; the meanings are given above.

words_with_history.title: Dal latino all'italiano
text: Forse cui Guido vostro ebbe a disdegno: disdegno = sdegno.
Guardommi un poco, e poi quasi sdegnoso.
Lo strazio e il grande scempio.
words_with_history.note_en: Latin dedignari, 'to think unworthy' (de + dignus), was remade in spoken Latin with the commoner prefix dis-: *disdignare. Italian kept both shapes of the prefix: in full in disdegno (line 63), shrunk to s- before a consonant in sdegno, sdegnoso (line 41) and Compagni's sdegnare (lesson 15). The same prefix s- (from dis- or ex-) makes scoperchiata (line 52, 'uncovered', from coperchio, Latin cooperculum). The pair in line 85 are older words whose s- came with the whole word's development, not as a prefix added in Italian. Strazio probably derives from distractio, 'a pulling apart', which became 'torment, mangling'. Scempio comes from exemplum: a punishment that served as an example to others, then any savage cruelty or slaughter. Exemplum also gave the semi-learned esempio, which keeps more of the Latin shape (though -pl- has become -pi-, as in popular words): one Latin word, two routes, two meanings. The other Latin of the canto lies on the surface: arca for a stone coffin, carcer, loquela, magnanimus, supinus, natus 'son'; and Epicurus, known to the Middle Ages mainly through Cicero, as the man who denied the soul's survival.

A.title: A
A.instruction: Rispondi in inglese o in italiano.

items.prompt: Che cosa domanda Farinata a Dante? Che cosa risponde Dante su «quell'arte»?
model_answers: Domanda chi furono i padri di Dante, per sapere di quale casa e di quale parte è. Poi dice che li cacciò due volte; Dante risponde che i suoi tornarono tutte e due le volte, ma quelli di Farinata non sanno l'arte di tornare.
items.rubric: Lines 40–51: Farinata asks who Dante's ancestors were, to place him by family and party; on hearing, he says they were fierce enemies of his house and party and he scattered them twice. Dante answers that they came back both times, but Farinata's people never learned that art (the art of returning from exile). Credit noting the irony: Dante himself will need that art.

model_answers: Dante dice «ebbe»: è un tempo per le cose passate e chiuse, e Cavalcante crede che Guido sia morto. Dante non risponde subito, e per lui il silenzio è una risposta.
items.rubric: Lines 58–72: Cavalcante asks why Guido, as gifted as Dante, is not with him; Dante's answer says Guido 'ebbe a disdegno'. The remote past makes the father believe, wrongly, that Guido's life is over; when Dante delays his reply, he takes the silence as confirmation and falls back. Credit any answer that names the tense.

B.title: B
B.instruction: Rispondi in inglese o in italiano.

items.prompt: Che cosa dice Farinata del futuro di Dante, e che cosa fece Farinata per Firenze?
model_answers: Fra poco più di quattro anni Dante saprà quanto pesa l'arte di tornare: anche lui sarà esule, e non potrà tornare. Dopo Montaperti, Farinata solo difese Firenze, quando tutti volevano che Firenze non ci fosse più.
items.rubric: Lines 79–93: before the moon is rekindled fifty times (about four years), Dante will learn how heavy that art is: his own exile and failed return (usual reading: the exiles' defeat of 1304). Farinata adds that at Montaperti he was not alone and had cause, but at the council afterwards (Empoli) he alone defended Florence openly when all agreed to destroy it.

items.prompt: Che cosa sanno i morti del futuro e del presente? Che cosa domanda Dante a Farinata di dire a Cavalcante?
model_answers: Vedono le cose lontane, come chi vede male da vicino; delle cose vicine o presenti sanno solo quello che altri raccontano loro. Dante fa dire a Cavalcante che suo figlio è ancora vivo, e che tacque perché non capiva.
items.rubric: Lines 97–114: the damned see the future from afar, like a long-sighted man, by God's light; what is near or present escapes them unless someone brings them news (e s'altri nol ci apporta, 104), and after the Last Judgment they will know nothing. Require the exception. Dante asks Farinata to tell 'that fallen one' that his son is still among the living, and that he was silent only because of this doubt.

C.title: C
C.instruction: Dal latino all'italiano. Answer in English or Italian. (1) Compare Latin dedignari (from dignus) with Italian disdegnare/disdegno and sdegnare/sdegno: what has happened to the prefix? (2) Latin exemplum gave both esempio and scempio (and distractio probably gave strazio). How did the sense move from 'example' to 'slaughter'?

items.prompt: Dante scrive «disdegno» e «sdegnoso»; anche Dino scrisse «disdegnate» e «sdegnare». Da dove viene la prima lettera di «sdegnoso»?
model_answers: Viene dal dis di disdegno: in disdegno c'è tutto, in sdegno e sdegnoso resta solo la prima lettera.
items.rubric: Sees that Latin de- in dedignari was replaced by dis- (*disdignare, whence disdegnare and the noun disdegno), which survives whole in disdegno and shrinks to s- before a consonant in sdegno, sdegnoso, sdegnare. Credit scoperchiata (ex- or dis- + coperchio) as a further s- word from the canto.

items.prompt: «Lo strazio e il grande scempio»: scempio ed esempio vengono dalla stessa parola. Come?
model_answers: Prima lo scempio era una pena che tutti dovevano vedere, come un esempio; poi fu ogni grande male fatto a molti, come a Montaperti.
items.rubric: exemplum: a punishment made an example of (exemplary punishment), then any savage cruelty or slaughter; esempio is the semi-learned twin of the same word, closer to the Latin shape. strazio probably < distractio, 'a tearing apart'. Credit any good account of the shift from 'example' through 'exemplary punishment' to 'massacre'.

provenance.author: Claude Opus 5.5 (capstone lesson 18, swarm writer, 2026-11-08)
notes: SOURCE. Dante Alighieri, La Divina Commedia, ed. Carl Witte, vol. I, Berlin: R. Decker, 1862 (archive.org ladivinacommedi03wittgoog), Inferno X on pp. 63–68 (63: 1–18; 64: 19–42; 65: 43–66; 66: 67–90; 67: 91–114; 68: 115–136). Transcribed line by line from the page images (leaves n163–n168) on 2026-11-08, with the archive.org OCR only as a first draft; OCR misreadings corrected from the scan (e.g. fii → fu, DaUa → Dalla, lome kept as printed); punctuation at lines 100, 109, 131 and 135 re-checked on 3000-px page images after the reviews. The whole canto is given unchanged: no cuts.

NORMALISATION. Words, accents and punctuation are Witte's (martìri, Josaffàt, perchè, Nè, no quotation marks). Two display changes only, as in chapter 14: verse lines are joined with line breaks inside one segment per tercet (the last segment holds 133–136); and Witte's space after an elision apostrophe is closed up (l' anima → l'anima, D' una → D'una, Rispos' io → Rispos'io), while truncated words that stand alone keep their space (I' avea, fu' io, Prega' io, a' miei, co' vivi, E' par).

FRAME. The two introductory sections and the short lead lines before each canto section are course Italian, not marked quotation. They recall chapter 6 (Guido rides ahead of the Sarzana group and looks at no one; returns with fever in August and dies at the end of the month; Lapo looks for 'l'amico di Cavalcanti' among the mourners but has never seen his face; Dante's name under the decree with the other priors) and the sentences of 1302 (chapters 11 and 13).

FACTS. Farinata (died 1264; condemned post mortem with his wife Adaleta by the inquisitor Salomone da Lucca, 1283); Montaperti 4 September 1260 and the council of Empoli; Guelf expulsions 1248 and 1260, returns 1251 and 1267; Cavalcante de' Cavalcanti, Guelf, Boccaccio's Epicurean (Enciclopedia Dantesca, 'Cavalcante de' Cavalcanti'); Guido's marriage to Farinata's daughter (Beatrice degli Uberti) in the peace of the 1260s; Dante prior 15 June – 14 August 1300 and Guido's death at the end of August 1300 (docs/it-dante-research.md). The fifty moons are given as the usual reading (spring 1300 to mid-1304), and the cui of line 63 as the commonest of the usual readings, with the alternatives in the note.

EXERCISES. As in lesson 15: A and B hold four self-check reading questions in source order (A: 22–51, 52–72; B: 73–93, 94–114), C the two Dal latino transfer items, with the Latin only in C's English instruction and rubrics.

BRIDGE STRINGS. Appended to course.json bridge_references.la for this lesson's Latin margin glosses (each a real Latin form with the sense used): callis, loquela, arca, maiores, mecum, carcer, supinus, magnanimus, natus. (sententia was already there.)

LICENSING. Integrated on origin/main after chapters 1–14 and lessons 15–17 were published: known vocabulary is the real lexicon.json. The canto's rare and archaic words are new receptive_only lexemes; forms of earlier chapters' lexemes first met here are listed under those ids with this lesson as the form's first_lesson. check.mjs: 0 errors after integration.

OVERLAPS. Lower chapter wins: words this lesson shares with chapters 1–17 (among them capo, costa, dinanzi, intelletto, intero and vano from lesson 16; tomba, ombra, duca, maestro, dolce and others from lesson 17; pronto from chapter 13) keep their earlier first_lesson here. This lesson first uses gire, lassù, lume, mutare, piegare, raggio, ripensare and satisfare, which lesson 19's draft delta also declares; 19 should re-date them to l18.

WARNINGS LEFT. Coordinator ruling (2026-11-08, all capstones): any word that occurs only inside quoted verse is receptive_only, even a common one; so 63 of this lesson's 65 new lexemes are receptive_only and only eretico and verbo, used in the frame, are ordinary (both recur three times). The remaining recurrence warnings all concern receptive_only words confined to the canto (the COURSE.md exception); forms of other chapters' lexemes that occur only in the verse are marked receptive_only at form level. media-coverage: new nouns without a picture; the capstone plans no images (plan row media: none).

TAP GLOSSES. Default entries for every new token were added to glosses/forms.json; glosses/capitolo-18.json carries the occurrence-specific senses where the shared default misfits this canto: empi (impious, not empiere), arte (art of return, not guild), E' (it), legge (law), regge in line 82 (may you return), letto (bed, line 78), sentenza (opinion), quei (one who), passi (steps), li/gli/il as pronouns, nato (son), Appresso (then), Cardinale (Ottaviano degli Ubaldini).
LENGTH. About 1,660 running words (window 1,300–2,500, target 1,900 advisory): about 960 words of verse and 700 of course Italian. Not padded.

review_questions.question: RQ18-1 [?] Witte against Petrocchi (card: record, do not adopt). Substantive differences: 10 Ed egli / E quelli; 14 tutti i suoi / tutti suoi; 17 sarai / sarà; 27 forse io fui / forse fui; 33 cintura / cintola; 36 in gran dispitto / a gran dispitto; 42 fur / fuor; 44 tutti gliel'apersi / tutto gliel'apersi; 45 soso / suso; 57 il suspicar / 'l sospecciar; 62 Colui, che attende / colui ch'attende (comma); 68 egli ebbe… viv'egli / elli ebbe… viv'elli; 69 lome / lume; 76 E se, continuando / e sé continüando; 91 sol colà / solo, là; 92 toglier / tòrre; 97 E' par / El par; 104 nol / non; 112 innanzi / dianzi; 113 Fat'ei saper / fate i saper; 117 con lui stava / con lu' istava; 123 nimico / nemico; 133 volse / mosse. Orthographic only (not listed one by one): della / de la, Ed io / E io, satisfammi / sodisfammi, Josaffàt / Iosafàt, lassù / là sù, cor / cuor, perchè / perché, Nè / né, no quotation marks in Witte. RQ18-3 [?] Line 63, cui: the margin follows one usual reading (Virgil leads Dante toward Beatrice, whom Guido disdained) and names it in the reveal; the note gives the alternatives (God; Virgil himself). Is the owner content with Beatrice in the margin?

RQ18-4 [?] Line 79, fifty moons: given as the usual reading (spring 1300 + 50 months ≈ mid-1304, the exiles' failure that summer). Line 132 says Beatrice will tell Dante of his life's journey; in the poem Cacciaguida tells him in detail, at Beatrice's prompting (Paradiso XVII); the grammar note now says so.

RQ18-5 [?] The introduction says the two Florentines speak 'da una di queste tombe' and that Cavalcante rises beside Farinata: the usual reading of 'lungo questa' (52–53) is that they share one tomb. Witte line 21 shows a mark over the first i of disposto (a print flaw, transcribed disposto).

RQ18-6 [?] Line 118–120 margin: 'il re Federico secondo' (Frederick II was emperor and king of Sicily); imperatore is not a licensed word, so the English reveal says Emperor. Line 135 fiede glossed in the tap gloss as 'strikes; here: leads down into'.

RQ18-7 [?] For the coordinator or owner: common Italian words met first in the canto and nowhere else in this lesson (collo, mento, petto, valle, nodo, raggio, viso, cintura, ginocchio, cimitero, conoscenza, apprendere, piegare, pronto, rosso, sentiero, sinistro, sorgere, sospirare, spegnere, virtù, lassù, muto) are declared ordinary lexemes, as the card asks, and so carry recurrence warnings; a reading of Dante cannot repeat them without padding. Decision needed: broaden the capstone exception to ordinary words confined to quotations (lesson 15 left about 55 such warnings), or mark them receptive_only in capstones.
